\textbf{Why spatial supervision can improve task success without improving safety.} The disconnect between TSR and CAR has a structural explanation. On SafeLIBERO Level~I, 7 of 10 tasks already exhibit CAR $\geq$ 0.92 under the Vanilla baseline, leaving little room for spatial supervision to improve safety on these tasks (ceiling effect). The remaining 3 tasks with high collision rates (43--93\%) involve tight spatial constraints where collisions arise from physical proximity between the manipulation target and obstacles, not from a lack of spatial awareness. Auxiliary spatial prediction can help the policy locate objects (benefiting task completion) without teaching it to avoid contact in geometrically constrained configurations. Spatial supervision thus addresses a different bottleneck than the one that drives collision failures.

\textbf{Statistical power.} The $2{\times}2$ factorial design prioritizes breadth (12 conditions, 5 factors) over per-cell statistical power. For the BN row, the observed effect size is large (Hedges' $g{=}-0.781$), but with $n{=}3$ vs.\ $n{=}4$ seeds per cell, post-hoc power is approximately 0.3--0.4~\cite{cohen1988statistical}, meaning there is a 60--70\% probability of failing to detect a true effect of this magnitude at $\alpha{=}0.05$. We report this limitation transparently. However, the study's evidential strength does not rest on any single pairwise comparison. The directional consistency across all twelve conditions---every configuration performs at or below Vanilla---yields $p < 0.001$ under a binomial null (probability 0.5 of improvement), providing strong global evidence that auxiliary spatial supervision does not improve collision avoidance. Seed expansion ($n{=}5$ per factorial cell) is underway to increase per-cell power.

\textbf{Practical guideline.} Do not add auxiliary spatial heads for the purpose of improving collision avoidance; all tested configurations perform at or below the Vanilla baseline.

Guidelines: do not add auxiliary spatial heads for safety; if required by other objectives, use Detach+LN and never combine BatchNorm with gradient flow (no ground-truth labels needed, zero inference cost).

CKA analysis confirms that encoder representations remain intact under all conditions (CKA $\geq$ 0.95), localizing the safety degradation to the optimization trajectory rather than representational capacity. Because the problem lies in how auxiliary gradients reshape LoRA updates rather than in what spatial information the labels encode, training schedule design and loss balancing are more promising levers than label content for safety-relevant outcomes. More broadly, training-time collision avoidance may require approaches that directly encode safety constraints---such as constrained optimization~\cite{zhang2025safevla} or safety-aware reward shaping---rather than auxiliary prediction tasks that improve spatial awareness without shaping the policy's collision behavior.
